title: Τηλεμάχου παρρησία
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Book 1 ends in the hall on Ithaca. As Phemius the bard sings of the Achaeans’ bitter homecomings, Penelope comes down from her chamber in tears and asks him to stop, but her son Telemachus, newly sure of himself, sends her back upstairs and claims the household’s authority as his own. He then turns on the suitors crowding his father’s hall, promising them a public reckoning at dawn and calling down the gods’ vengeance on them. Antinous and Eurymachus needle him in turn about the stranger who slipped away earlier that evening, not knowing it was Athena in disguise, and Telemachus answers them while privately understanding what they do not. The feast breaks up into song and dancing until dark, and the book closes with Telemachus in his room, undressed by his old nurse Eurycleia, lying awake to ponder the journey the goddess has set before him.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἀοιδὸς ἄειδε περικλυτός, οἱ δὲ σιωπῇ
ἥατ’ ἀκούοντες·
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ aoidos aeide periklytos, hoi de siōpēi
hēat’ akouontes·
sentences.l:
To them then the minstrel was singing, far-famed, and they in silence
sat listening;
sentences.i: The famous minstrel was singing to them, and they sat listening in silence;
sentences.n: ἀοιδὸς περικλυτός names Phemius, though not yet by name, with his standing epithet ’far-famed’. ἥατ’ is ἥατο, an epic perfect/imperfect of ἧμαι ’sit’ (Attic ἧντο), unaugmented; σιωπῇ ’in silence’ is a dative of manner. The bard sings on while the suitors feast, unaware of the grief his song is about to cause.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ Ἀχαιῶν νόστον ἄειδε
λυγρόν, ὃν ἐκ Τροίης ἐπετείλατο Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ Achaiōn noston aeide
lygron, hon ek Troiēs epeteilato Pallas Athēnē.
sentences.l:
and he of the Achaeans’ homecoming was singing,
bitter, which from Troy Pallas Athena laid upon them.
sentences.i: he was singing of the bitter homecoming of the Achaeans, which Pallas Athena had laid upon them, setting out from Troy.
sentences.n: νόστον...λυγρόν ’the bitter homecoming’ names the theme of the disastrous returns of the Greek chiefs after Troy (the story later called the Nostoi), distinct from Odysseus’s own νόστος. ἐπετείλατο is aorist middle of ἐπιτέλλω ’lay a charge upon, ordain’, with Athena as the agent who decreed the Achaeans’ sufferings — her anger at the sack of Troy, not told here. ἐκ Τροίης marks the point from which the doom took effect.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ὑπερωιόθεν φρεσὶ σύνθετο θέσπιν ἀοιδὴν
κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr:
tou d’ hyperōiothen phresi syntheto thespin aoidēn
kourē Ikarioio, periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l:
And his, from upstairs, in her mind took note of the god-given song,
the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope;
sentences.i: And from her room above, the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope, caught in her mind the sound of the god-given song;
sentences.n: ὑπερωιόθεν ’from the upper story’ uses the -θεν suffix of place from which; the women’s quarters lay upstairs (ὑπερῷον). σύνθετο is aorist middle of συντίθημι, ’perceived, took note of’. θέσπις ’god-given, inspired’ marks song as literally granted by a god. περίφρων ’circumspect’ is Penelope’s standing epithet, formed like πολύφρων but kept distinct for her alone (see new-renderings).

sentences.t:
κλίμακα δ’ ὑψηλὴν κατεβήσετο οἷο δόμοιο,
οὐκ οἴη, ἅμα τῇ γε καὶ ἀμφίπολοι δύ’ ἕποντο.
sentences.tr:
klimaka d’ hypsēlēn katebēseto hoio domoio,
ouk oiē, hama tēi ge kai amphipoloi dy’ heponto.
sentences.l:
And down the high staircase she came, of her own house,
not alone; with her, indeed, two handmaids also followed.
sentences.i: She came down the high staircase of her own house, not alone; two handmaids went with her.
sentences.n: κατεβήσετο is an unaugmented sigmatic aorist middle of καταβαίνω, ’she came down’ (Attic κατέβη). οἷο is the possessive pronoun in the genitive -οιο (= Attic οὗ), ’her own’, agreeing with δόμοιο. ἀμφίπολος ’handmaid, attendant’ recurs for Penelope’s and later Eurycleia’s women through this part.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ὅτε δὴ μνηστῆρας ἀφίκετο δῖα γυναικῶν,
στῆ ῥα παρὰ σταθμὸν τέγεος πύκα ποιητοῖο,
ἄντα παρειάων σχομένη λιπαρὰ κρήδεμνα·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ hote dē mnēstēras aphiketo dia gynaikōn,
stē rha para stathmon tegeos pyka poiētoio,
anta pareiaōn schomenē lipara krēdemna·
sentences.i: When she reached the suitors, she, heavenly among women, stood by the doorpost of the well-built hall, holding her shining veil before her cheeks;
sentences.n: δῖα γυναικῶν follows the pattern of δῖα θεάων in the house-rendering table, a partitive genitive with δῖα ’heavenly’ (see new-renderings, since δῖα γυναικῶν is not itself in the table). σταθμός is the door-post; τέγος ’roof’ stands for the hall as a whole. Holding the κρήδεμνον, the head-veil, before the cheeks is the mark of a modest woman appearing among men.

sentences.t: ἀμφίπολος δ’ ἄρα οἱ κεδνὴ ἑκάτερθε παρέστη.
sentences.tr: amphipolos d’ ara hoi kednē hekaterthe parestē.
sentences.l: and a trusty handmaid then, on each side of her, stood by.
sentences.i: and on either side of her a trusty handmaid took her stand.
sentences.n: κεδνή ’careful, trusty’ recurs of Eurycleia later in this part (κεδνὰ ἰδυῖα, 1.428). ἀμφίπολος is grammatically singular, yet ἑκάτερθε ’on each side’ implies that one of the two handmaids named at 1.331 took each side — Greek can use a singular noun distributively like this.

sentences.t: δακρύσασα δ’ ἔπειτα προσηύδα θεῖον ἀοιδόν·
sentences.tr: dakrysasa d’ epeita prosēuda theion aoidon·
sentences.l: and weeping, then, she addressed the divine minstrel:
sentences.i: and in tears she then spoke to the divine minstrel:
sentences.n: δακρύσασα, aorist participle of δακρύω ’weep’, is concessive-temporal, ’having burst into tears’. θεῖος ’divine, god-inspired’ describes a poet’s gift of song as coming directly from a god, kept distinct from δῖος ’heavenly’, reserved for Odysseus (see new-renderings for θεῖος ἀοιδός). προσηύδα, imperfect of προσαυδάω, introduces the speech that follows; Murray prints no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
Φήμιε, πολλὰ γὰρ ἄλλα βροτῶν θελκτήρια οἶδας,
ἔργ’ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε, τά τε κλείουσιν ἀοιδοί·
sentences.tr:
Phēmie, polla gar alla brotōn thelktēria oidas,
erg’ andrōn te theōn te, ta te kleiousin aoidoi·
sentences.l:
“Phemius, for many other things, charms for mortals, you know,
deeds of men and of gods, which minstrels celebrate;
sentences.i: “Phemius, you know many other things to charm mortals with, deeds of men and gods, which minstrels make famous;
sentences.n: Φήμιε, vocative of Φήμιος, names the bard for the first time. θελκτήρια ’charms, means of enchantment’, from θέλγω ’bewitch’, stands in apposition to ἄλλα. κλείουσιν ’celebrate, make famous’ shares its root with ἐπικλείουσι at 1.351. ἔργ’ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε echoes the shape of the formula πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε, here naming epic’s ordinary subject matter.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἕν γέ σφιν ἄειδε παρήμενος, οἱ δὲ σιωπῇ
οἶνον πινόντων·
sentences.tr:
tōn hen ge sphin aeide parēmenos, hoi de siōpēi
oinon pinontōn·
sentences.l:
of these, one at least to them sing, sitting beside them, and let them in silence
drink their wine;
sentences.i: sing them just one of these, sitting near them, and let them drink their wine in silence;
sentences.n: ἕν...τῶν is a partitive genitive, ’one out of these many things’. παρήμενος ’sitting beside’ pictures the bard settled among the diners as he sings, an easy conversational posture. πινόντων is a third-person plural imperative (Attic πινέτωσαν), ’let them drink’.

sentences.t:
ταύτης δ’ ἀποπαύε’ ἀοιδῆς
λυγρῆς, ἥ τέ μοι αἰεὶ ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλον κῆρ
τείρει, ἐπεί με μάλιστα καθίκετο πένθος ἄλαστον.
sentences.tr:
tautēs d’ apopaue’ aoidēs
lygrēs, hē te moi aiei eni stēthessi philon kēr
teirei, epei me malista kathiketo penthos alaston.
sentences.l:
but from this song cease,
the bitter one, which always in my breast my own heart
wears down, since upon me above all has come sorrow not to be forgotten.
sentences.i: but stop this bitter song, which forever wears down the heart in my breast, since a grief I cannot forget has come upon me more than upon anyone;
sentences.n: ἀποπαύε(ο) is a present middle imperative, ’cease from’ + genitive. λυγρῆς, agreeing with ἀοιδῆς, repeats λυγρόν from 1.327 — the same word marks the song both times Penelope objects to it. στήθεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι. ἄλαστος ’unforgettable’, from ἀ- + λανθάνομαι, describes grief that never fades.

sentences.t:
τοίην γὰρ κεφαλὴν ποθέω μεμνημένη αἰεί,
ἀνδρός, τοῦ κλέος εὐρὺ καθ’ Ἑλλάδα καὶ μέσον Ἄργος.
sentences.tr:
toiēn gar kephalēn potheō memnēmenē aiei,
andros, tou kleos eury kath’ Hellada kai meson Argos.
sentences.l:
for such a head do I long for, remembering it always,
the man’s, whose fame is wide through Hellas and mid-Argos.”
sentences.i: for such is the man I long for and remember always, a man whose fame reaches wide through Hellas and the heart of Argos.”
sentences.n: κεφαλήν ’head’ stands by synecdoche for the whole person, an affectionate use close to English ’dear soul’. μεμνημένη is a perfect middle participle of μιμνήσκομαι, ’having in mind’. Ἑλλάς here names a district of Thessaly, not yet all Greece, and μέσον Ἄργος names the Argive plain — both narrower, older senses of names later used for the whole land.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This line is identical to 1.213 of odyssey-003 and keeps that ratified English, per the sole-source rule for repeated units. πεπνυμένος ’prudent’, a perfect participle of πέπνυμαι (root sense ’to breathe, be conscious’), is Telemachus’s fixed epithet throughout the poem.

sentences.t:
μῆτερ ἐμή, τί τ’ ἄρα φθονέεις ἐρίηρον ἀοιδὸν
τέρπειν ὅππῃ οἱ νόος ὄρνυται;
sentences.tr:
mēter emē, ti t’ ara phthoneeis eriēron aoidon
terpein hoppēi hoi noos ornytai;
sentences.l:
“My mother, why then do you begrudge the trusty minstrel
to give delight wherever his mind is stirred?
sentences.i: “My mother, why do you begrudge our trusty minstrel the chance to give pleasure however his mind moves him?
sentences.n: φθονέεις is uncontracted (Attic φθονεῖς), ’begrudge’, with accusative and infinitive. ἐρίηρος ’trusty, well-fitted’, of uncertain root, elsewhere pairs with ἑταῖρος ’companion’; here it is given to the bard. ὅππῃ is epic for ὅπῃ, ’in whatever way’. This opens Telemachus’s first rebuke of his mother in the poem.

sentences.t:
οὔ νύ τ’ ἀοιδοὶ
αἴτιοι, ἀλλά ποθι Ζεὺς αἴτιος, ὅς τε δίδωσιν
ἀνδράσιν ἀλφηστῇσιν, ὅπως ἐθέλῃσιν, ἑκάστῳ.
sentences.tr:
ou ny t’ aoidoi
aitioi, alla pothi Zeus aitios, hos te didōsin
andrasin alphēstēisin, hopōs ethelēisin, hekastōi.
sentences.l:
Not, surely, are the minstrels
to blame, but Zeus, somehow, is to blame, who gives
to bread-eating men, as he wishes, to each.
sentences.i: It is not the minstrels who are to blame, but Zeus, somehow, who gives to bread-eating men, to each as he wishes.
sentences.n: αἴτιοι...αἴτιος repeats the word for emphasis. ἀλφηστής ’bread-eating’ (from ἄλφι ’barley’) marks mortal men as grain-eaters, as opposed to gods or monsters. ὅς τε, with the epic generalizing τε, states a standing truth about Zeus’s dispensations; ἐθέλῃσιν is a subjunctive in -ῃσι.

sentences.t: τούτῳ δ’ οὐ νέμεσις Δαναῶν κακὸν οἶτον ἀείδειν·
sentences.tr: toutōi d’ ou nemesis Danaōn kakon oiton aeidein·
sentences.l: and with this man there is no cause for indignation, the Danaans’ evil fate to sing;
sentences.i: and there is no reproach in his singing of the Danaans’ evil fate;
sentences.n: νέμεσις ’righteous indignation, blame’ governs the dative τούτῳ, ’against this man’. Δαναοί is one of Homer’s three names for the Greeks, with Ἀχαιοί and Ἀργεῖοι. οἶτος ’fate, doom’ is regularly an evil one in Homer, here made explicit by κακόν.

sentences.t:
τὴν γὰρ ἀοιδὴν μᾶλλον ἐπικλείουσ’ ἄνθρωποι,
ἥ τις ἀκουόντεσσι νεωτάτη ἀμφιπέληται.
sentences.tr:
tēn gar aoidēn mallon epikleious’ anthrōpoi,
hē tis akouontessi neōtatē amphipelētai.
sentences.l:
for that song the more men extol,
whichever, to the listeners, newest goes around.
sentences.i: for men praise more whatever song is newest to reach the ears of the listener.
sentences.n: ἐπικλείουσι ’extol, make famous’ shares its root with κλείουσιν at 1.338. ἀκουόντεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι of the participle, ’those listening’. ἀμφιπέληται, present subjunctive of ἀμφιπέλομαι ’circulate’, is drawn into the mood of the indefinite relative clause. The claim that novelty draws an audience is a small piece of literary theory in Telemachus’s mouth.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ ἐπιτολμάτω κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀκούειν·
sentences.tr: soi d’ epitolmatō kradiē kai thymos akouein·
sentences.l: but let your heart and spirit endure to listen;
sentences.i: so let your heart and spirit steel themselves to listen;
sentences.n: ἐπιτολμάτω, a third-person imperative of ἐπιτολμάω ’have the endurance for’, governs the infinitive ἀκούειν. κραδίη and θυμός, near-synonyms for the seat of feeling, are paired for emphasis, as often in Homer.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς οἶος ἀπώλεσε νόστιμον ἦμαρ
ἐν Τροίῃ, πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ ἄλλοι φῶτες ὄλοντο.
sentences.tr:
ou gar Odysseus oios apōlese nostimon ēmar
en Troiēi, polloi de kai alloi phōtes olonto.
sentences.l:
for not Odysseus alone lost the homecoming day
at Troy, but many other men besides perished.
sentences.i: for Odysseus was not the only one to lose his day of homecoming at Troy; many other men perished too.
sentences.n: νόστιμον ἦμαρ, ’the homecoming day’, is the house-rendering used of Odysseus at the poem’s opening; here Telemachus applies it to his father with grim irony, as a day already lost rather than merely delayed. ἀπώλεσε is aorist of ἀπόλλυμι. φῶτες, plural of φώς ’man, hero’, is a poetic word distinct from ἀνήρ.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰς οἶκον ἰοῦσα τὰ σ’ αὐτῆς ἔργα κόμιζε,
ἱστόν τ’ ἠλακάτην τε, καὶ ἀμφιπόλοισι κέλευε
ἔργον ἐποίχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
all’ eis oikon iousa ta s’ autēs erga komize,
histon t’ ēlakatēn te, kai amphipoloisi keleue
ergon epoichesthai·
sentences.i: Go instead into the house and attend to your own work, the loom and the distaff, and tell your handmaids to get on with their tasks;
sentences.n: κόμιζε is a present imperative, ’take care of’. τὰ σ’ αὐτῆς ἔργα, ’your own works’, marks the loom and distaff as a wife’s proper sphere, set against the μῦθος that follows. ἱστός ’loom’ and ἠλακάτη ’distaff’ are the standard tools of Homeric women’s work; ἐποίχεσθαι ’go about, ply’ takes ἔργον as its object.

sentences.t:
μῦθος δ’ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει
πᾶσι, μάλιστα δ’ ἐμοί·
sentences.tr:
mythos d’ andressi melēsei
pasi, malista d’ emoi·
sentences.l:
but speech shall be the men’s concern,
all of them, and mine above all;
sentences.i: speech will be the concern of men, of all of them, and mine most of all;
sentences.n: μελήσει, future of μέλω ’be a care to’, governs the dative ἄνδρεσσι impersonally: ’speech will be a care to the men’. This line draws the sharp line between women’s domestic ἔργα and men’s public μῦθος that runs through the whole poem’s picture of the household.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ κράτος ἔστ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ.
sentences.tr: tou gar kratos est’ eni oikōi.
sentences.l: for the mastery is mine within the house.”
sentences.i: for the authority in this house is mine.”
sentences.n: τοῦ is the genitive of ὁ, ἡ, τό, the demonstrative/personal pronoun (not the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν), used here with possessive force, ’his’; its reference loops back to Telemachus himself, echoing ἐμοί just before, a normal Homeric resumptive shift from first to third person. κράτος ’strength, mastery, authority’ used of household headship marks Telemachus’s claim, on coming of age, to rule his father’s house. This closes his speech to Penelope.

sentences.t: ἡ μὲν θαμβήσασα πάλιν οἶκόνδε βεβήκει·
sentences.tr: hē men thambēsasa palin oikonde bebēkei·
sentences.l: She, then, astonished, had gone back again homeward;
sentences.i: Astonished, she went back again to her chamber;
sentences.n: θαμβήσασα, aorist participle of θαμβέω ’be astonished’, marks Penelope’s reaction to her son’s newly firm tone. βεβήκει, pluperfect of βαίνω with simple past force (the so-called Homeric pluperfect), is the ordinary way the narrative moves a character offstage.

sentences.t: παιδὸς γὰρ μῦθον πεπνυμένον ἔνθετο θυμῷ.
sentences.tr: paidos gar mython pepnymenon entheto thymōi.
sentences.l: for her son’s prudent speech she laid to heart.
sentences.i: for she took to heart her son’s prudent words.
sentences.n: πεπνυμένον here modifies μῦθον, not Telemachus himself: the adjective normally attached to the man is transferred to his speech, ’a speech showing sound sense’. ἔνθετο, aorist middle of ἐντίθημι, with dative θυμῷ, is a formula for taking something seriously to heart.

sentences.t:
ἐς δ’ ὑπερῷ’ ἀναβᾶσα σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξὶ
κλαῖεν ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆα φίλον πόσιν, ὄφρα οἱ ὕπνον
ἡδὺν ἐπὶ βλεφάροισι βάλε γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr:
es d’ hyperōi’ anabasa syn amphipoloisi gynaixi
klaien epeit’ Odysēa philon posin, ophra hoi hypnon
hēdyn epi blepharoisi bale glaukōpis Athēnē.
sentences.l:
And up to the upper chamber having gone, with her attendant women,
she wept then for Odysseus, her dear husband, until upon her sleep,
sweet, upon her eyelids cast gleaming-eyed Athena.
sentences.i: She went up to her upper room with her attendant women and wept then for Odysseus, her dear husband, until gleaming-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep upon her eyelids.
sentences.n: ὑπερῷα, plural of ὑπερῷον, is the upstairs chamber named already at 1.328 (ὑπερωιόθεν). κλαῖεν is an unaugmented imperfect of continued weeping. ὄφρα here means ’until’ with the indicative βάλε, marking the point the weeping actually stops — sleep sent by the goddess, not simply natural, ends Penelope’s grief for the night.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρες δ’ ὁμάδησαν ἀνὰ μέγαρα σκιόεντα,
πάντες δ’ ἠρήσαντο παραὶ λεχέεσσι κλιθῆναι.
sentences.tr:
mnēstēres d’ homadēsan ana megara skioenta,
pantes d’ ērēsanto parai lecheessi klithēnai.
sentences.l:
And the suitors made an uproar throughout the shadowy hall,
and all of them prayed beside her to lie down.
sentences.i: The suitors broke into uproar throughout the shadowy hall, and every one of them prayed to lie down at her side.
sentences.n: ὁμάδησαν, aorist of ὁμαδέω ’make a din’, breaks in as soon as Penelope withdraws. σκιόεντα ’shadowy, dim’ describes the great hall. ἠρήσαντο, aorist middle of ἀράομαι ’pray, wish’, with παραὶ λεχέεσσι κλιθῆναι ’to lie down beside her bed’, makes the suitors’ desire for Penelope explicit; the poem does not soften it.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἤρχετο μύθων·
sentences.tr: toisi de Tēlemachos pepnymenos ērcheto mythōn·
sentences.l: and among them prudent Telemachus began to speak:
sentences.i: and prudent Telemachus began to speak among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι δὲ...ἤρχετο μύθων, ’began to address them’, is a formal, elevated way to open a speech, marking Telemachus’s coming words to the suitors as a weighty public address rather than a private word. πεπνυμένος is his fixed epithet again.

sentences.t:
μητρὸς ἐμῆς μνηστῆρες ὑπέρβιον ὕβριν ἔχοντες,
νῦν μὲν δαινύμενοι τερπώμεθα, μηδὲ βοητὺς
ἔστω, ἐπεὶ τόδε καλὸν ἀκουέμεν ἐστὶν ἀοιδοῦ
τοιοῦδ’ οἷος ὅδ’ ἐστί, θεοῖς ἐναλίγκιος αὐδήν.
sentences.tr:
mētros emēs mnēstēres hyperbion hybrin echontes,
nyn men dainymenoi terpōmetha, mēde boētys
estō, epei tode kalon akouemen estin aoidou
toioud’ hoios hod’ esti, theois enalinkios audēn.
sentences.l:
“Suitors of my mother, having overweening insolence,
now, feasting, let us take our pleasure, and let there be no shouting;
since this is a fine thing, to listen to a minstrel
such as this one is, one like the gods in voice.
sentences.i: “Suitors of my mother, you with your overbearing insolence, for now let us feast and enjoy ourselves, and let there be no clamor; for it is a fine thing to listen to a minstrel such as this man is, one whose voice is like the gods’.
sentences.n: ὑπέρβιον ὕβριν pairs a strengthened adjective with ὕβρις, the poem’s key moral term, applied to the suitors here for the first time; it becomes their standing charge throughout. βοητύς ’shouting, clamor’ is a rare noun from βοάω. ἐναλίγκιος + dative, ’like, resembling’, with αὐδήν an accusative of respect, ’in voice’, pays Phemius a striking compliment.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν δ’ ἀγορήνδε καθεζώμεσθα κιόντες
πάντες, ἵν’ ὕμιν μῦθον ἀπηλεγέως ἀποείπω,
ἐξιέναι μεγάρων·
sentences.tr:
ēōthen d’ agorēnde kathezōmestha kiontes
pantes, hin’ hymin mython apēlegeōs apoeipō,
exienai megarōn·
sentences.i: and at dawn let us all go and take our seats in assembly, so that I may tell you plainly and without softening to leave this hall;
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν ’at dawn’ uses the -θεν suffix of place or time from which. καθεζώμεσθα is a hortatory subjunctive. ἀπηλεγέως ’bluntly, without regard for consequence’ modifies ἀποείπω, an aorist subjunctive of ἀπεῖπον ’declare formally’ — the first announcement of the assembly that opens Book 2. ἐξιέναι μεγάρων depends on ἀποείπω, ’to declare that you go forth’.

sentences.t:
ἄλλας δ’ ἀλεγύνετε δαῖτας,
ὑμὰ κτήματ’ ἔδοντες, ἀμειβόμενοι κατὰ οἴκους.
sentences.tr:
allas d’ alegynete daitas,
hyma ktēmat’ edontes, ameibomenoi kata oikous.
sentences.l:
but see to other feasts,
eating your own possessions, taking turns through your houses.
sentences.i: and go and hold your feasts elsewhere, eating up what is your own, moving from house to house in turn.
sentences.n: ἀλεγύνετε, present imperative of ἀλεγύνω ’take care of, prepare’ (a feast). ὑμὰ ’your own’ (= ὑμέτερα) is pointed against the suitors’ habit of consuming Telemachus’s household goods. ἀμειβόμενοι κατὰ οἴκους, ’taking turns from house to house’, names the proper way for men to feast at one another’s expense, not permanently at one man’s.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ὕμιν δοκέει τόδε λωίτερον καὶ ἄμεινον
ἔμμεναι, ἀνδρὸς ἑνὸς βίοτον νήποινον ὀλέσθαι,
κείρετ’·
sentences.tr:
ei d’ hymin dokeei tode lōiteron kai ameinon
emmenai, andros henos bioton nēpoinon olesthai,
keiret’·
sentences.i: But if it seems to you more profitable and better to waste one man’s living without paying for it, then go on and devour it;
sentences.n: λωίτερον and ἄμεινον, ’more advantageous’ and ’better’, are near-synonyms piled up for scorn. νήποινος ’unavenged, without penalty’ names the outcome the suitors are gambling on. κείρετ(ε), literally ’shear, crop’, here ’strip bare’, gives the suitors the harsh image of grazing animals stripping an estate.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δὲ θεοὺς ἐπιβώσομαι αἰὲν ἐόντας,
αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς δῷσι παλίντιτα ἔργα γενέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
egō de theous epibōsomai aien eontas,
ai ke pothi Zeus dōisi palintita erga genesthai·
sentences.l:
but I will call upon the gods who are forever,
if somehow Zeus may grant that deeds requited-in-turn come to pass;
sentences.i: but I will call upon the gods who are forever, in hope that Zeus may somehow grant that there be a reckoning for what you have done;
sentences.n: θεοὺς...αἰὲν ἐόντας is the house-rendering ’the gods who are forever’. ἐπιβώσομαι, future of ἐπιβοάομαι ’call upon, invoke’. παλίντιτα ἔργα ’deeds paid back in turn’, built on the root of τίσις, names the vengeance Telemachus hopes for, anticipating the poem’s ending.

sentences.t: νήποινοί κεν ἔπειτα δόμων ἔντοσθεν ὄλοισθε.
sentences.tr: nēpoinoi ken epeita domōn entosthen oloisthe.
sentences.l: then unavenged, within the house, may you all perish.”
sentences.i: then may you all perish inside this house, unavenged.”
sentences.n: νήποινοι, again ’without requital’, now falls on the suitors themselves — a grim symmetry with νήποινον of line 377. ὄλοισθε, an aorist optative of wish (2nd pl.) of ὄλλυμι, is a direct curse that closes Telemachus’s speech to the suitors.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ὀδὰξ ἐν χείλεσι φύντες
Τηλέμαχον θαύμαζον, ὃ θαρσαλέως ἀγόρευεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes odax en cheilesi phyntes
Tēlemachon thaumazon, ho tharsaleōs agoreuen.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then, all of them, on their lips having bitten,
marveled at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all of them, biting their lips, marveled at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
sentences.n: ὀδὰξ ἐν χείλεσι φύντες, literally ’having grown their teeth into their lips’, is a vivid formula for suppressed anger or astonishment; φύντες is the aorist participle of φύω used almost adverbially. θαρσαλέως ’boldly’ echoes back to the same adverb Antinous will use sarcastically against Telemachus at 1.385.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντίνοος προσέφη, Εὐπείθεος υἱός·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Antinoos prosephē, Eupeitheos huios·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Antinous, Eupeithes’ son:
sentences.i: Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A new reply-formula for this part: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’...προσέφη with name and patronymic, distinct from the πεπνυμένος-formula for Telemachus and from τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη in the house-rendering table (see new-renderings). Antinous is named here for the first time in the poem, with his father Eupeithes; he leads the suitors’ hostility throughout.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, ἦ μάλα δή σε διδάσκουσιν θεοὶ αὐτοὶ
ὑψαγόρην τ’ ἔμεναι καὶ θαρσαλέως ἀγορεύειν·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemach’, ē mala dē se didaskousin theoi autoi
hypsagorēn t’ emenai kai tharsaleōs agoreuein·
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, truly indeed the gods themselves are teaching you
to be a lofty speaker, and to speak boldly;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, the gods themselves are certainly teaching you to talk big and to speak boldly;
sentences.n: ὑψαγόρης ’high-talking, big-mouthed’ (ὕψι + ἀγορεύω) is a rare, plainly mocking compound. ἔμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί. θαρσαλέως picks up the narrator’s own word from 1.382, now turned into a sneer.

sentences.t:
μὴ σέ γ’ ἐν ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ βασιλῆα Κρονίων
ποιήσειεν, ὅ τοι γενεῇ πατρώιόν ἐστιν.
sentences.tr:
mē se g’ en amphialōi Ithakēi basilēa Kroniōn
poiēseien, ho toi geneēi patrōion estin.
sentences.l:
may the son of Cronus not make you, at least, in sea-girt Ithaca king,
which is yours by birth, your father’s due.”
sentences.i: may the son of Cronus not make you king in sea-girt Ithaca, a thing that is yours by birth, your father’s right.”
sentences.n: ἀμφίαλος Ἰθάκη ’sea-girt Ithaca’ (ἀμφί ’around’ + ἅλς ’sea’) is a new formula in this part, recurring at 1.395 and 1.401 and rendered the same way each time (see new-renderings). Κρονίων is a by-form of Κρονίδης, Zeus. ποιήσειεν is an aorist optative of wish. πατρώιος ’hereditary’ names Telemachus’s rightful claim, voiced by Antinous only to mock it.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is the same reply-formula as 1.345, with the pronoun changed from feminine τήν (to Penelope) to masculine τόν (to a suitor); the line recurs verbatim at 1.412 to Eurymachus, and both take the same English, since repeated Greek within a part keeps the same rendering.

sentences.t: Ἀντίνο’, ἦ καί μοι νεμεσήσεαι ὅττι κεν εἴπω;
sentences.tr: Antino’, ē kai moi nemesēseai hotti ken eipō;
sentences.l: “Antinous, will you indeed be angry with me for whatever I may say?
sentences.i: “Antinous, will you truly be indignant with me over whatever I say?
sentences.n: νεμεσήσεαι is a future middle with the uncontracted ending -εαι (Attic νεμεσήσῃ), from the root of νέμεσις at 1.350. ὅττι is the epic doubled form of ὅτι; κεν with the subjunctive εἴπω gives the indefinite sense ’whatever I might say’.

sentences.t: καί κεν τοῦτ’ ἐθέλοιμι Διός γε διδόντος ἀρέσθαι.
sentences.tr: kai ken tout’ etheloimi Dios ge didontos aresthai.
sentences.l: This too I would be willing, Zeus at least granting it, to win.
sentences.i: I would be glad to win even this, if only Zeus would grant it.
sentences.n: ἐθέλοιμι is an optative of hypothetical wish. Διός...διδόντος is a genitive absolute, ’Zeus granting it’. ἀρέσθαι, aorist middle infinitive of ἄρνυμαι ’win, gain’ (the verb of the poem’s own proem), shows Telemachus answering Antinous’s sarcasm about kingship by saying he would gladly take it, were it the god’s gift.

sentences.t: ἦ φῂς τοῦτο κάκιστον ἐν ἀνθρώποισι τετύχθαι;
sentences.tr: ē phēis touto kakiston en anthrōpoisi tetychthai;
sentences.l: Or do you say that this is the worst thing to have come about among men?
sentences.i: Or do you claim this is the worst thing that can happen to a man?
sentences.n: φῄς is second person singular of φημί. τετύχθαι, a perfect passive infinitive of τεύχω, ’to have come to be’, gives the periphrasis typical of epic diction for plain ’is’. κάκιστον is a superlative, ’worst’.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι κακὸν βασιλευέμεν·
sentences.tr: ou men gar ti kakon basileuemen·
sentences.l: For it is no bad thing at all to be king;
sentences.i: For to be a king is no bad thing at all;
sentences.n: βασιλευέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν, the epic ending noted in the conventions (compare ἐριδαινέμεν), from βασιλεύω ’be king, rule’. οὐ...τι is ’not at all’, the same idiom used elsewhere in this part (e.g. οὐ μὲν γάρ τι κακῷ, 1.411). Telemachus turns Antinous’s taunt about kingship into an argument for the position, before pointedly declining to claim it for himself.

sentences.t:
αἶψά τέ οἱ δῶ
ἀφνειὸν πέλεται καὶ τιμηέστερος αὐτός.
sentences.tr:
aipsa te hoi dō
aphneion peletai kai timēesteros autos.
sentences.l:
quickly, too, his house
wealthy becomes, and he himself more honored.
sentences.i: quickly his household grows wealthy, and he himself gains more honor.
sentences.n: αἶψα ’quickly’ with the generalizing τε. δῶ is a rare shortened form of δῶμα, ’house’. πέλεται, present of πέλομαι ’become, be’, is used almost as a synonym for γίγνεται. τιμηέστερος is a comparative of τιμήεις ’honored’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι βασιλῆες Ἀχαιῶν εἰσὶ καὶ ἄλλοι
πολλοὶ ἐν ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ, νέοι ἠδὲ παλαιοί,
τῶν κέν τις τόδ’ ἔχῃσιν, ἐπεὶ θάνε δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr:
all’ ē toi basilēes Achaiōn eisi kai alloi
polloi en amphialōi Ithakēi, neoi ēde palaioi,
tōn ken tis tod’ echēisin, epei thane dios Odysseus·
sentences.i: But there are plenty of other Achaean kings besides, many of them, in sea-girt Ithaca, young and old alike, and one of them may well have this position, now that heavenly Odysseus is dead;
sentences.n: βασιλῆες...πολλοί points to a plurality of local chieftains on Ithaca rather than a single hereditary throne, a detail of early Greek kingship. ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ recurs a second time (see 1.386). δῖος, of Odysseus, is the house-rendering ’heavenly’, kept distinct from θεῖος ’divine’ (compare 1.336). ἔχῃσιν is again a subjunctive in -ῃσι.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν οἴκοιο ἄναξ ἔσομ’ ἡμετέροιο
καὶ δμώων, οὕς μοι ληίσσατο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.tr:
autar egōn oikoio anax esom’ hēmeteroio
kai dmōōn, hous moi lēissato dios Odysseus.
sentences.l:
but I myself will be lord of our own house
and of the slaves whom for me heavenly Odysseus won as spoil.”
sentences.i: but I at least will be lord of our own house and of the slaves that heavenly Odysseus won for me as spoil.”
sentences.n: ἄναξ ’lord, master’ is the modest but firm claim Telemachus stakes, in contrast to the βασιλεύς ’king’ that Antinous mocked him with: he claims mastery of his own household, not the wider kingship. ληίσσατο, aorist middle of ληίζομαι ’take as booty’, from ληίς ’spoil’, recalls that some of Odysseus’s slaves were won in war. This closes Telemachus’s reply to Antinous.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Εὐρύμαχος Πολύβου πάϊς ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Eurymachos Polybou païs antion ēuda·
sentences.l: Him then in turn spoke Eurymachus, Polybus’ son, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A second new reply-formula in this part, combining Antinous’s introductory αὖτ’ with Telemachus’s closing ἀντίον ηὔδα (see new-renderings). Eurymachus is introduced here, by name and patronymic, for the first time; with Antinous he leads the suitors through the rest of the poem.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, ἦ τοι ταῦτα θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται,
ὅς τις ἐν ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ βασιλεύσει Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemach’, ē toi tauta theōn en gounasi keitai,
hos tis en amphialōi Ithakēi basileusei Achaiōn·
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, truly these things lie on the knees of the gods,
whoever of the Achaeans shall be king in sea-girt Ithaca;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, this indeed lies on the knees of the gods, which of the Achaeans is to be king in sea-girt Ithaca;
sentences.n: θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται is the house-rendering ’lie(s) on the knees of the gods’, a formula for what fate has not yet decided. βασιλεύσει is a future loosely governed by the indefinite ὅς τις. ἀμφιάλῳ Ἰθάκῃ appears for the third time in this part (compare 1.386, 1.395).

sentences.t: κτήματα δ’ αὐτὸς ἔχοις καὶ δώμασιν οἷσιν ἀνάσσοις.
sentences.tr: ktēmata d’ autos echois kai dōmasin hoisin anassois.
sentences.l: but your possessions may you yourself keep, and over your own house may you be lord.
sentences.i: but may you yourself keep your possessions and be lord in your own house.
sentences.n: ἔχοις and ἀνάσσοις are both optatives of wish, not commands: Eurymachus concedes Telemachus’s household authority while withholding any wider claim. δώμασιν οἷσιν, ’in his own halls’, again uses the possessive ὅς.

sentences.t:
μὴ γὰρ ὅ γ’ ἔλθοι ἀνὴρ ὅς τίς σ’ ἀέκοντα βίηφιν
κτήματ’ ἀπορραίσει, Ἰθάκης ἔτι ναιετοώσης.
sentences.tr:
mē gar ho g’ elthoi anēr hos tis s’ aekonta biēphin
ktēmat’ aporraisei, Ithakēs eti naietoōsēs.
sentences.l:
for may that man never come, whoever, against your will, by force
shall strip away your possessions, while Ithaca is still inhabited.
sentences.i: for may there never come a man who will strip your goods from you by force against your will, while Ithaca is still a place men live in.
sentences.n: ἔλθοι is an optative of wish (negative μή) with βίηφιν, an instrumental in -φι(ν), the suffix of means noted in the conventions. ναιετοώσης, a genitive absolute participle with diectasis (uncontracted -όω- for -ῶ-), ’while it is still inhabited’, is an oddly ominous qualification, as if inhabited Ithaca could not simply be assumed.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐθέλω σε, φέριστε, περὶ ξείνοιο ἐρέσθαι,
ὁππόθεν οὗτος ἀνήρ, ποίης δ’ ἐξ εὔχεται εἶναι
γαίης, ποῦ δέ νύ οἱ γενεὴ καὶ πατρὶς ἄρουρα.
sentences.tr:
all’ ethelō se, pheriste, peri xeinoio eresthai,
hoppothen houtos anēr, poiēs d’ ex euchetai einai
gaiēs, pou de ny hoi geneē kai patris aroura.
sentences.l:
But I wish, best of men, to ask you about the stranger,
from where this man is, and from what land he claims
to be, and where, then, is his family and his fatherland’s soil.
sentences.i: But I want to ask you, best of men, about the stranger — where this man is from, and what land he claims to come from, and where his family and his native soil are.
sentences.n: φέριστε, a vocative superlative of φέρτατος ’best, bravest’, is used here with heavy irony. ἐρέσθαι is an aorist middle infinitive of ἔρομαι ’ask’. εὔχεται ’claims, boasts’, governing εἶναι, is the verb regularly used in Homer for a man’s own account of his origin, presented rather than verified. πατρὶς ἄρουρα, ’the ancestral ploughland’, pictures a homeland as farmed soil.

sentences.t:
ἠέ τιν’ ἀγγελίην πατρὸς φέρει ἐρχομένοιο,
ἦ ἑὸν αὐτοῦ χρεῖος ἐελδόμενος τόδ’ ἱκάνει;
sentences.tr:
ēe tin’ angeliēn patros pherei erchomenoio,
ē heon autou chreios eeldomenos tod’ hikanei;
sentences.l:
Or does he bring some message of your father’s coming,
or, his own business here desiring, has he come for this?
sentences.i: Does he bring some news of your father’s coming, or has he come here seeking some business of his own?
sentences.n: ἀγγελίην...πατρὸς ἐρχομένοιο, ’a message of the father’s coming’, uses a genitive participle much as English ’news that the father is coming’. ἑὸν αὐτοῦ χρεῖος, ’his own affair’, pairs the possessive ἑόν with αὐτοῦ for emphasis. ἐελδόμενος, a participle of ἔλδομαι ’desire’, is reduplicated for the meter.

sentences.t:
οἷον ἀναΐξας ἄφαρ οἴχεται, οὐδ’ ὑπέμεινε
γνώμεναι·
sentences.tr:
hoion anaïxas aphar oichetai, oud’ hypemeine
gnōmenai·
sentences.l:
How suddenly, having sprung up, he is gone at once, nor did he wait
to be known;
sentences.i: How suddenly he sprang up and was gone at once, without waiting to be recognized;
sentences.n: οἷον is exclamatory, ’how!’, as elsewhere in the poem. ἀναΐξας is an aorist participle of ἀναΐσσω ’start up suddenly’. οἴχεται is a present with perfect sense, ’is gone’. γνώμεναι, an epic infinitive in -μεναι of γιγνώσκω, ’to be known’, marks Eurymachus’s notice of the stranger’s suspiciously abrupt departure — the audience already knows it was Athena.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι κακῷ εἰς ὦπα ἐῴκει.
sentences.tr: ou men gar ti kakōi eis ōpa eōikei.
sentences.l: for he did not look, in his face, at all like a base man.”
sentences.i: for he did not look at all like a lowborn man to judge by his face.”
sentences.n: ἐῴκει is a pluperfect of ἔοικα with imperfect force, ’resembled, looked like’. εἰς ὦπα, ’as to his face’, is an accusative of respect. κακῷ, dative, is ’a base, ignoble man’ — Eurymachus reads good breeding from appearance, unaware he is describing a goddess.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This line repeats 1.388 exactly and so keeps the same English, per the rule that Greek repeated within a part is rendered identically both times.

sentences.t: Εὐρύμαχ’, ἦ τοι νόστος ἀπώλετο πατρὸς ἐμοῖο·
sentences.tr: Eurymach’, ē toi nostos apōleto patros emoio·
sentences.l: “Eurymachus, truly my father’s homecoming has been lost;
sentences.i: “Eurymachus, my father’s homecoming is indeed lost and gone;
sentences.n: ἀπώλετο, aorist middle of ἀπόλλυμι, echoes the active ἀπώλεσε of 1.354, but now says the νόστος itself, not merely the day, has perished — Telemachus’s bleakest statement yet about his father’s prospects.

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ οὖν ἀγγελίῃ ἔτι πείθομαι, εἴ ποθεν ἔλθοι,
οὔτε θεοπροπίης ἐμπάζομαι, ἥν τινα μήτηρ
ἐς μέγαρον καλέσασα θεοπρόπον ἐξερέηται.
sentences.tr:
out’ oun angeliēi eti peithomai, ei pothen elthoi,
oute theopropiēs empazomai, hēn tina mētēr
es megaron kalesasa theopropon exereētai.
sentences.l:
neither, then, in a message do I trust any longer, should one come from anywhere,
nor of a prophecy do I take heed, whatever one my mother,
into the hall having called a soothsayer, may inquire of.
sentences.i: I no longer put any trust in a message, should one come from anywhere, nor do I pay heed to any prophecy my mother may seek out, calling a soothsayer into the hall to ask.
sentences.n: ἀγγελίῃ πείθομαι, ’trust in a message’, takes a dative object. θεοπροπίη ’a prophetic utterance’ and θεοπρόπος ’a soothsayer’ share the same root and are deliberately repeated together. ἐξερέηται is a subjunctive in a relative clause of indefinite reference. Telemachus voices a weary skepticism of both rumor and formal divination alike.

sentences.t:
ξεῖνος δ’ οὗτος ἐμὸς πατρώιος ἐκ Τάφου ἐστίν,
Μέντης δ’ Ἀγχιάλοιο δαΐφρονος εὔχεται εἶναι
υἱός, ἀτὰρ Ταφίοισι φιληρέτμοισιν ἀνάσσει.
sentences.tr:
xeinos d’ houtos emos patrōios ek Taphou estin,
Mentēs d’ Anchialoio daïphronos euchetai einai
huios, atar Taphioisi philēretmoisin anassei.
sentences.l:
But this stranger is my guest-friend from my father’s time, from Taphos,
and Mentes, of wise-minded Anchialus, claims to be
the son, but over the oar-loving Taphians he rules.”
sentences.i: This stranger of mine is a guest-friend from my father’s time, from Taphos, and he claims to be Mentes, son of wise-hearted Anchialus, and he rules over the oar-loving Taphians.”
sentences.n: πατρώιος ξεῖνος is the house-rendering ’a guest-friend from my/our fathers’ time’. δαΐφρων, here of Anchialus, repeats the disputed epithet already given to Odysseus (’wise-minded’, from δαῆναι, the doubt noted on its first occurrence). φιλήρετμος ’oar-loving’ is the house-rendering for the seafaring, piratical Taphians. Telemachus does not reveal here that he privately knows the stranger was a goddess — that comes only in the narrator’s voice at 1.420.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο Τηλέμαχος, φρεσὶ δ’ ἀθανάτην θεὸν ἔγνω.
sentences.tr: hōs phato Tēlemachos, phresi d’ athanatēn theon egnō.
sentences.l: So spoke Telemachus, but in his mind he recognized the immortal goddess.
sentences.i: So Telemachus spoke, though in his heart he knew it was an immortal goddess.
sentences.n: φρεσὶ...ἔγνω, ’knew in his mind’, reveals to the audience — but not to the suitors — that Telemachus has privately understood his visitor Mentes was a god, confirming what the reader already knew from Athena’s disguised visit earlier in the book. ἔγνω is the unaugmented aorist of γιγνώσκω, the same verb as γνώμεναι at 1.411, now given its object.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ εἰς ὀρχηστύν τε καὶ ἱμερόεσσαν ἀοιδὴν
τρεψάμενοι τέρποντο, μένον δ’ ἐπὶ ἕσπερον ἐλθεῖν.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ eis orchēstyn te kai himeroessan aoidēn
trepsamenoi terponto, menon d’ epi hesperon elthein.
sentences.l:
And they to dancing and to lovely song
having turned, took their pleasure, and waited for evening to come.
sentences.i: The suitors turned to dancing and lovely song and took their pleasure in it, waiting for evening to come.
sentences.n: τρεψάμενοι, aorist middle participle of τρέπω, ’having turned [themselves]’. ἱμερόεσσαν ’lovely, desirable’ is from ἵμερος ’longing’. μένον...ἐλθεῖν, ’waited for evening to come’, uses the infinitive of the awaited event, a common construction after verbs of waiting.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ τερπομένοισι μέλας ἐπὶ ἕσπερος ἦλθε·
sentences.tr: toisi de terpomenoisi melas epi hesperos ēlthe·
sentences.l: and upon them, taking their pleasure, black evening came;
sentences.i: and as they enjoyed themselves, black evening came upon them;
sentences.n: μέλας ἕσπερος ’black evening’ is a vivid epithet for nightfall; μέλας elsewhere describes blood, ships’ pitch and the sea, so its use here carries a similarly heavy colour. τερπομένοισι, a dative participle, picks up τέρποντο from the line before.

sentences.t: δὴ τότε κακκείοντες ἔβαν οἶκόνδε ἕκαστος.
sentences.tr: dē tote kakkeiontes eban oikonde hekastos.
sentences.l: then indeed, to lie down going, each one went to his own house.
sentences.i: then at last each of them went off home to bed.
sentences.n: κακκείοντες is a future participle with reduplicated κ- (= κατακείοντες), ’intending to lie down’, expressing purpose. ἔβαν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω. ἕκαστος closes the evening’s feast as the suitors finally disperse.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’, ὅθι οἱ θάλαμος περικαλλέος αὐλῆς
ὑψηλὸς δέδμητο περισκέπτῳ ἐνὶ χώρῳ,
ἔνθ’ ἔβη εἰς εὐνὴν πολλὰ φρεσὶ μερμηρίζων.
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachos d’, hothi hoi thalamos perikalleos aulēs
hypsēlos dedmēto periskeptōi eni chōrōi,
enth’ ebē eis eunēn polla phresi mermērizōn.
sentences.l:
But Telemachus, where for him a chamber, of the very beautiful courtyard,
high, had been built, in a conspicuous place,
there he went to his bed, much in his mind pondering.
sentences.i: But Telemachus, where his chamber had been built high up, in a conspicuous spot within the very beautiful courtyard, went there to his bed, turning many things over in his mind.
sentences.n: δέδμητο is a pluperfect passive of δέμω ’build’, ’had been built’. περισκέπτῳ ’seen all around, conspicuous’ describes the chamber’s prominent position, a detail of the palace’s layout. μερμηρίζων ’pondering anxiously’ is a participle that regularly closes a scene on a note of inward deliberation, here anticipating the whole of Book 2.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἅμ’ αἰθομένας δαΐδας φέρε κεδνὰ ἰδυῖα
Εὐρύκλει’, Ὦπος θυγάτηρ Πεισηνορίδαο,
τήν ποτε Λαέρτης πρίατο κτεάτεσσιν ἑοῖσιν
πρωθήβην ἔτ’ ἐοῦσαν, ἐεικοσάβοια δ’ ἔδωκεν,
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ ar’ ham’ aithomenas daïdas phere kedna iduia
Euryklei’, Ōpos thygatēr Peisēnoridao,
tēn pote Laertēs priato kteatessin heoisin
prōthēbēn et’ eousan, eeikosaboia d’ edōken,
sentences.l:
And with him, then, burning torches carried the one wise and trusty,
Eurycleia, Ops’ daughter, Peisenor’s grandson,
whom once Laertes bought, with his own possessions,
while she was still in her first youth, and twenty oxen’s worth he gave,
sentences.i: With him went the trusty and wise Eurycleia, daughter of Ops son of Peisenor, carrying burning torches — the woman Laertes had once bought with his own wealth, when she was still in the first bloom of youth, giving the worth of twenty oxen for her,
sentences.n: κεδνὰ ἰδυῖα ’trusty, knowing in her heart’ is a new formula in this part for Eurycleia (see new-renderings), echoing κεδνή for the handmaid at 1.335 but intensified with ἰδυῖα, the perfect participle of οἶδα, ’skilled, wise’. Eurycleia is named here for the first time in the poem, her patronymic running through her grandfather Peisenor to her father Ops. ἐεικοσάβοιον ’worth twenty oxen’, a relic of a cattle-based valuation, is applied here to the purchase price of a slave.

sentences.t:
ἶσα δέ μιν κεδνῇ ἀλόχῳ τίεν ἐν μεγάροισιν,
εὐνῇ δ’ οὔ ποτ’ ἔμικτο, χόλον δ’ ἀλέεινε γυναικός·
sentences.tr:
isa de min kednēi alochōi tien en megaroisin,
eunēi d’ ou pot’ emikto, cholon d’ aleeine gynaikos·
sentences.l:
and equal to his trusty wife he honored her in the halls,
but in her bed he never mingled, and he avoided his wife’s anger;
sentences.i: and he honored her in his halls as much as his own trusted wife, but he never went to her bed, and so avoided his wife’s anger;
sentences.n: ἶσα...τίεν, ’honored her equally’, with the dative κεδνῇ ἀλόχῳ, leaves the comparison to be inferred from the dative alone. ἔμικτο, pluperfect middle of μίγνυμι, the verb regularly used of sexual union, is here negated: Laertes never took Eurycleia to his bed, out of tact toward his unnamed wife Anticleia.

sentences.t:
ἥ οἱ ἅμ’ αἰθομένας δαΐδας φέρε, καί ἑ μάλιστα
δμῳάων φιλέεσκε, καὶ ἔτρεφε τυτθὸν ἐόντα.
sentences.tr:
hē hoi ham’ aithomenas daïdas phere, kai he malista
dmōiaōn phileeske, kai etrephe tytthon eonta.
sentences.l:
she, with him, burning torches carried, and him most of all,
of the slave-women, she used to love, and she reared him when he was small.
sentences.i: she was the one who carried burning torches with him, and she loved him best of all the household women, and had nursed him when he was a small child.
sentences.n: αἰθομένας δαΐδας φέρε repeats exactly the phrase used of Eurycleia at 1.428, the part’s one internal repeated line noted in the packet; the same English, ’burning torches carried’, is kept both times. φιλέεσκε is an iterative imperfect in -εσκε, ’used to love’, marking habitual past action, a form that recurs through the poem (see new-renderings). ἔτρεφε ’reared, nursed’ establishes Eurycleia as Telemachus’s own childhood nurse.

sentences.t:
ὤιξεν δὲ θύρας θαλάμου πύκα ποιητοῖο,
ἕζετο δ’ ἐν λέκτρῳ, μαλακὸν δ’ ἔκδυνε χιτῶνα·
sentences.tr:
ōixen de thyras thalamou pyka poiētoio,
hezeto d’ en lektrōi, malakon d’ ekdyne chitōna·
sentences.l:
And he opened the doors of the close-built chamber,
and sat down on the bed, and took off his soft tunic;
sentences.i: He opened the doors of the well-built chamber, sat down on the bed, and took off his soft tunic;
sentences.n: ὤιξεν is an unaugmented aorist of οἴγνυμι ’open’. πύκα ποιητοῖο ’closely, well built’ repeats the phrase already used of Penelope’s chamber at 1.333 — the same formula recurs for different well-made rooms across the poem. ἔκδυνε is an imperfect of ἐκδύω ’strip off [clothing]’.

sentences.t: καὶ τὸν μὲν γραίης πυκιμηδέος ἔμβαλε χερσίν.
sentences.tr: kai ton men graiēs pykimēdeos embale chersin.
sentences.l: and it he cast into the hands of the wise old woman.
sentences.i: and he put it into the hands of the shrewd old woman.
sentences.n: πυκιμήδης ’close-witted, shrewd’ (πυκινός + μῆδος) is a further new epithet in this part for Eurycleia, distinct from κεδνὰ ἰδυῖα at 1.428; the poem gives her several such epithets of wise competence, each kept as its own plain rendering, as with the -φρων epithets in the table. ἔμβαλε χερσίν, ’threw into her hands’, is an easy, homely gesture as Telemachus undresses for bed.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν τὸν πτύξασα καὶ ἀσκήσασα χιτῶνα,
πασσάλῳ ἀγκρεμάσασα παρὰ τρητοῖσι λέχεσσι
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ἐκ θαλάμοιο, θύρην δ’ ἐπέρυσσε κορώνῃ
ἀργυρέῃ, ἐπὶ δὲ κληῖδ’ ἐτάνυσσεν ἱμάντι.
sentences.tr:
hē men ton ptyxasa kai askēsasa chitōna,
passalōi ankremasasa para trētoisi lechessi
bē rh’ imen ek thalamoio, thyrēn d’ eperysse korōnēi
argyreēi, epi de klēid’ etanyssen himanti.
sentences.l:
And she, the tunic having folded and having smoothed it,
on a peg having hung it up beside the bored bedstead,
went then to go out from the chamber, and the door she drew shut by its handle,
silver, and upon it the bolt she drew tight with a strap.
sentences.i: She folded the tunic and smoothed it out, hung it on a peg beside the corded bedstead, and went out of the chamber, drawing the door shut by its silver handle and pulling the bolt tight with its strap.
sentences.n: ἀσκήσασα, ’having worked smooth’, from ἀσκέω, describes finishing cloth by careful handling. τρητοῖσι λέχεσσι, ’bored bedsteads’, describes a frame strung with leather thongs through drilled holes, the ordinary Homeric bed. κορώνη ’handle, curved door-ring’ and κληΐς ’bolt’ with an ἱμάς ’strap’ describe the simple mechanism of a Homeric door, drawn shut from outside by a cord through the handle.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ὅ γε παννύχιος, κεκαλυμμένος οἰὸς ἀώτῳ,
βούλευε φρεσὶν ᾗσιν ὁδὸν τὴν πέφραδ’ Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr:
enth’ ho ge pannychios, kekalymmenos oios aōtōi,
bouleue phresin hēisin hodon tēn pephrad’ Athēnē.
sentences.l:
There he, all night long, covered with the fleece of a sheep,
pondered in his own mind the journey which Athena had pointed out.
sentences.i: There, all night long, wrapped in a fleece of wool, he pondered in his own mind the journey Athena had shown him.
sentences.n: οἰὸς ἀώτῳ, ’with the flower of a sheep’, is a kenning for fine wool used as a coverlet, ἄωτος properly ’flower, choicest part’. πέφραδε is a reduplicated aorist of φράζω ’point out, show’, of Athena’s counsel to Telemachus earlier in the book, in her disguise as Mentes. The book closes, as it opened, with a figure lying awake turning over what a god has set in motion.
